at regne.explanation: "At regne" means "to rain". "Det regner" (it rains) also means "it is raining", because Danish has no separate "is ...ing" form. "At regne" can also mean "to calculate": "Han regner hurtigt" (He calculates quickly).

sentence.en: It is raining all day today.

at rejse.explanation: "At rejse" means "to travel" or "to go away on a trip": "Jeg rejser til Danmark" (I am travelling to Denmark). In the "I have" form Danish uses "er" (am) instead of "har" (have): "Jeg er rejst" means "I have left" or "I have travelled". "En rejse" means "a trip".

sentence.en: I am travelling to Copenhagen tomorrow.

at ringe.explanation: "At ringe" means "to call" someone on the phone. You put "til" (to) before the person: "Jeg ringer til dig i morgen" (I will call you tomorrow). It also means "to ring", like a bell or a doorbell.

sentence.en: I will call you tomorrow.

at ringe op.explanation: "At ringe op" means "to call" someone on the phone. The person goes between the two parts: "Jeg ringer dig op" (I call you). It means the same as "ringe til" (to call): "Jeg ringer til dig".

sentence.en: I will call you tomorrow.

at ringe til.explanation: "At ringe til" means "to call" someone on the phone. You need "til" (to) before the person: "Jeg ringer til min mor" (I call my mother). "At ringe" on its own can also mean a bell ringing.

sentence.da: Jeg **ringer til** min mor i aften.
sentence.en: I'm calling my mom tonight.

en rabat.explanation: "En rabat" means "a discount", an amount taken off the price. You can ask "Kan jeg få rabat?" (Can I get a discount?), with no "en" in front of "rabat".

sentence.da: Får jeg **rabat**, hvis jeg køber to?
sentence.en: Do I get a discount if I buy two?

en radio.explanation: "En radio" means "a radio". Danish says "i radioen" (literally "in the radio") where English says "on the radio", as in "Det var i radioen" (It was on the radio).

sentence.en: I listen to the radio in the car.

en recept.explanation: "En recept" means "a prescription", the note from a doctor that you take to the pharmacy to get medicine. It does not mean a cooking recipe: that is "en opskrift" (a recipe).

sentence.da: Jeg skal have en **recept** fra lægen.
sentence.en: I need a prescription from the doctor.

en regning.explanation: "En regning" means "a bill", at a restaurant or at home, for example for electricity. In a restaurant you can ask politely "Må jeg bede om regningen?" (May I ask for the bill?).

sentence.en: May I have the bill?

en regnjakke.explanation: "En regnjakke" means "a rain jacket". It is "regn" (rain) and "jakke" (jacket) joined into one word, and Danish makes many words this way, so you can often guess new ones.

sentence.en: Take your rain jacket with you, it is raining.

en regnskov.explanation: "En regnskov" means "a rainforest". It is "regn" (rain) and "skov" (forest) joined into one word, and it takes "en" because "en skov" (a forest) does.

sentence.da: Det regner hele året i en **regnskov**.
sentence.en: It rains all year in a rainforest.

en reje.explanation: "En reje" means "a shrimp", also called a prawn. Danes eat them on bread as "rejemad" (shrimp on bread), usually with mayonnaise.

sentence.da: Jeg vil have **rejer** på mit brød.
sentence.en: I want shrimps on my bread.

en rejse.explanation: "En rejse" means "a trip" or "a journey", usually a longer one such as a holiday abroad. For a short outing Danes say "en tur" (a trip, a walk). The same word is also the verb "at rejse" (to travel), and "God rejse!" means "Have a good trip!".

sentence.en: We have a trip to Spain.

en reservation.explanation: "En reservation" means "a reservation", for example for a table, a train seat or a hotel room. You can say "Jeg har en reservation" (I have a reservation) or "at bestille bord" (to book a table).

sentence.en: I have a reservation tonight.

en restaurant.explanation: "En restaurant" means "a restaurant", a place where you sit down and have a meal. To say you eat out, Danes say "at spise på restaurant" (to eat at a restaurant), with no "en" after "på".

sentence.en: We are eating at a restaurant tonight.

en returbillet.explanation: "En returbillet" means "a return ticket", one that takes you there and back. The opposite is "en enkeltbillet" (a one-way ticket). At a counter you can say "En returbillet til Aarhus, tak." (A return ticket to Aarhus, please.)

sentence.en: A return ticket to Aarhus, please.

en rose.explanation: "En rose" means "a rose", the flower. The colour word "rosa" (pink) comes from it, so pink is named after roses.

sentence.en: He gave her a rose.

en ryg.explanation: "En ryg" means "a back", the back of your body. Danish says "the back" where English says "my back": "Jeg har ondt i ryggen" (literally "I have pain in the back") means "My back hurts". "At ligge på ryggen" means "to lie on your back".

sentence.en: My back hurts.

en rygsæk.explanation: "En rygsæk" means "a backpack". It is "ryg" (back) and "sæk" (sack) joined into one word, and you use it for school, hiking and travel.

sentence.en: I have the books in my backpack.

en rødvin.explanation: "En rødvin" means "a red wine". It is "rød" (red) and "vin" (wine) joined into one word. You usually order it by the glass or bottle: "et glas rødvin" (a glass of red wine) or "en flaske rødvin" (a bottle of red wine).

sentence.da: Jeg tager et glas **rødvin** til maden.
sentence.en: I will have a glass of red wine with the meal.

et rundstykke.explanation: "Et rundstykke" means "a bread roll", a small round roll of bread, often eaten at breakfast with butter, cheese or jam.

sentence.en: I eat a bread roll with cheese.

rask.explanation: "Rask" means "healthy" or "well again", especially after being ill. "Jeg er rask igen" means "I am well again", and "at blive rask" means "to get well". It can also mean quick and lively, as in "et raskt tempo" (a brisk pace). The opposite is "syg" (sick).

sentence.en: I hope you get well soon.

regn.explanation: "Regn" means "rain", the weather itself, so there is no "a rain". To say that it is raining, Danish uses an action word instead: "Det regner" (It is raining).

sentence.en: A lot of rain comes in the autumn.

regnvejr.explanation: "Regnvejr" means "rainy weather". It is built from "regn" (rain) and "vejr" (weather). You hear "Det er regnvejr" (It is rainy weather) or "i regnvejr" (in rainy weather) on days when you need an umbrella.

sentence.en: We stay at home in rainy weather.

rejer.explanation: "Rejer" means "shrimp" or "prawns", and you mostly hear it in this "more than one" form. "En rejemad" (a shrimp sandwich) is a classic open sandwich, often with mayonnaise.

sentence.en: I love shrimp with lemon.

ren.explanation: "Ren" means "clean", and also "pure", as in "rent vand" (clean water) or "ren luft" (clean air). The opposite is "beskidt" or "snavset" (both mean dirty). "At gøre rent" (to clean) is the everyday way to say you are cleaning the house.

sentence.en: Is your room clean?

reserveret.explanation: "Reserveret" means "reserved" and comes from "at reservere" (to reserve). It also describes people: a "reserveret" person is reserved, a little distant and keeps to themselves.

sentence.en: This table is reserved.

resten.explanation: "Resten" means "the rest", whatever is left over. It is often used with "af" (of): "resten af maden" (the rest of the food). The "the" is already built into the end of "resten", so you add nothing more.

sentence.en: You can have the rest of the cake.

rig.explanation: "Rig" means "rich", with a lot of money, but also rich in other things: "en rig historie" is "a rich story". The opposite is "fattig" (poor). Do not mix it up with "et rige" (a kingdom), which looks almost the same.

sentence.en: She has become very rich.

rigtig.explanation: "Rigtig" means "correct" or "right", as in "et rigtigt svar" (a correct answer). It also means "real" or "proper": "en rigtig cowboy" is "a real cowboy". In casual speech it can mean "really": "rigtig god" (really good). The opposite is "forkert" (wrong).

sentence.en: Is this the right way?

ris.explanation: "Ris" means "rice". You use it without "a", as in "Jeg spiser ris" (I eat rice) or "kylling og ris" (chicken and rice).

sentence.en: We eat rice for dinner.

rolig.explanation: "Rolig" means "calm" or "relaxed", and "peaceful" or "quiet" for places. "Vær rolig" means "Stay calm" or "Calm down". "Roligt" also means "calmly": "Tal roligt" (Speak calmly). The opposite is "urolig" (restless, worried).

sentence.en: She is always so calm.

rugbrød.explanation: "Rugbrød" means "rye bread", the dark, heavy bread that is typical in Denmark. It is built from "rug" (rye) and "brød" (bread). It is the base for "smørrebrød" (open sandwiches).

sentence.en: I eat rye bread for lunch.

forms.en: the bakery is around the corner

forms.da: Julen er lige rundt om hjørnet
forms.en: Christmas is just around the corner

rundt om hjørnet.explanation: "Rundt om hjørnet" means "around the corner" and works both literally and figuratively, just like in English. It is built from "rundt" (around), "om" (about) and "hjørnet" (the corner). Add "lige" (just) to say "just around the corner".

sentence.en: The post office is just around the corner.

rusland.explanation: "Rusland" means "Russia". A person from there is "en russer" (a Russian) and the language is "russisk" (Russian). Many country names end in "-land", like "Finland", "Tyskland" (Germany) and "Island" (Iceland).

sentence.en: Russia is a big country.

russisk.explanation: "Russisk" means "Russian", for the language and for things from Russia. Unlike English, it is written with a small letter: "russisk", not "Russisk". A person is "en russer" (a Russian) and the country is "Rusland" (Russia).

sentence.en: He can read Russian.

rød.explanation: "Rød" means "red". You meet it in food words: "rødvin" (red wine) and "rød pølse" (a bright red Danish hot dog).

sentence.da: Jeg kan godt lide den **røde** jakke.
sentence.en: I like the red jacket.
